extracted.intended_audience: civil-service_examiners, education_policy_makers, and school/college teachers involved in designing or reforming competitive public-service examinations (British/India context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for the place, design, and scoring of language, literature, history, and science components in competitive Civil Service examinations; proposes how to test ends (English composition, reasoning, history) rather than means (translation/grammar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Languages not proper subjects for competition for professional appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: My thesis, then, is that languages are not a proper subject for competition with a view to professional appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a foreign language is not used in actual business of the post, it should not be a competitive subject; even if languages produce valuable indirect benefits (culture, reasoning), those ends should be tested directly in their own departments rather than by awarding competitive marks for knowledge of languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make job-essential spoken languages a pass/fail (absolute) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first place, there are certain avocations where a foreign language must be known, because it has to be used in actual business ... in such cases the knowledge of the language ... must be made imperative. This ... is not a case for competition, but for a sufficient pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set an absolute minimum standard (sufficient pass) for languages indispensable to duties (e.g., Indian spoken dialects). Do not award relative merit in competition for such baseline skills; reward practical advantage (e.g., earlier readiness for work) by other means (monetary prize), not by higher ranking in the competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay for results, not for means (assess ends directly)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle is a plain and obvious one. It is the payment for results, without inquiring into the means. The ends themselves are to be looked to, and not the means or instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the aim is good English composition, reason, or taste, examine those end-competencies directly (e.g., give marks in English, logic, or history) rather than giving credit because a candidate learned them via Latin/Greek; instruments (Latin, Greek) are only one of several means and should not be privileged in scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach and examine English composition, philology, logic, and taste as distinct subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to teach thorough English you need to arrange a course of English, allot a definite time to it ... If you wish to teach philology, provide a systematic scheme ... So for logic and for taste: these subjects are far too serious to be imparted in passing allusions while the pupil is engaged in struggling with enigmatic difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide dedicated courses and examinations for each intended competency rather than relying on incidental gains from language instruction; examinations should reward demonstrated ability in those specific domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical-language exams overemphasize translation/grammar; reform needed
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical, or language, teacher ... excellence in teaching is held by them to consist, in the first instance, in the power of accurate interpretation ... while the literature and history parts are small and of real worth is mainly the history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike out translation/grammatical emphasis that serves only the obsolete primary use; consider reallocating marks toward history (political institutions) and literature, or testing literary competence without requiring translation from originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested mark distribution for classics: 500 history, 250 literature
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to do full justice to classical antiquity, I would allow the present markings to continue, at the rate of 500 for political institutions and history, and 250 for literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If classical subjects remain, give priority to history/institutions (political philosophy/sociology) over language/translation; literature retains value but should be smaller than history in the scheme suggested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish language-examination in modern languages; examine literature instead
rubrics_metrics.description: In like manner, I would abolish the language-examination in modern languages, and give 250 marks for the literature of each of the three modern languages—French, German, Italian. The history would be taken as modern history, with an adequate total value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For modern languages allow merit for literary examination (which may be satisfied via translations or originals) and remove the barrier of requiring detailed grammatical/translation competence in the foreign tongue; place modern history under a separate examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature exams should test discrimination and power, not vocabulary/translation
rubrics_metrics.description: The examination, as before, should test the discrimination and the power, and not the vocabulary, of the languages themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design literary questions that probe critical discernment, taste, and literary judgment (these may be answered using translations or in the candidate's own language), rather than testing facility in translating or reciting foreign vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current literature questions are often meagre and compilatory (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Such an examination is, in the first place, a most meagre view of literature ... it is chiefly a matter of compilation from English sources; the actual readings of the candidate in Greek and Latin would be of little account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid literature/history questions that merely invite compilation from secondary English sources; create substantive literary-critical tasks that genuinely exercise judgment and familiarity rather than rote recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate language-instrument tests with assessment of other faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: When the teaching of classics is justified by secondary uses (good English, universal grammar, logic, taste), the teaching practice is not in full consistency therewith ... the mass of teachers can do very little in any of those directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the aim is to cultivate reasoning, taste, or English style, those should be explicitly taught and tested; do not rely on language instruction to deliver these complex secondary outcomes indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow indispensable preparatory studies to be required where they contribute to final professional ends
rubrics_metrics.description: There are certain indispensable preparatory studies—anatomy, physiology, and materia medica—such studies are made part of the examination, because they contribute to the testing for the final end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a preparatory subject is genuinely necessary for professional competence, include it as a required/assessed part of the examination; distinguish these legitimate cases from instruments that are merely one means among many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit overly-wide optionality that permits narrow-specialism winners
rubrics_metrics.description: No one subject is obligatory; and the choice is so wide that by a very narrow range of acquirements a man may sometimes succeed ... I find the case of a man entering the India service by force of languages alone, which I cannot but think a miscarriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the examination scheme requires breadth: candidates should represent multiple regions of study (sciences, English composition, humanities) and the scheme should prevent success by narrow specialization (e.g., languages alone or mathematics alone) without adequate competence elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require minimum thresholds across three broad study regions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are, I should say, three great regions of study that should be fairly represented by every successful candidate. The first is the sciences as a whole ... The second is English composition ... The third is ... the humanities, meaning the department of institutions and history, with perhaps literature ... In every one of these three departments I would fix a minimum below which the candidate must not fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set explicit minimum scores (thresholds) in sciences, English composition, and humanities/history/literature so that all successful candidates demonstrate balanced competence across these essential regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern-history should be centralized rather than fragmented among language examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of partitioning modern European history among the language-examiners for English, French, German, Italian, it would be better to relieve them of history altogether, and place the subject as a whole in the bands of a distinct examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidate history testing under a dedicated examiner to avoid patchy or duplicated history teaching/examination tied to language papers; this allows coherent assessment of modern history as an independent subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise specification of claimed 'secondary uses' required
rubrics_metrics.description: It is quite necessary ... to find terms more definite and tangible than the slippery words 'culture' and 'training'; we must know in precise language what particular powers or aptitudes are increased by the study of a foreign language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defenders claim languages produce indirect benefits (mental training, culture), require them to specify the concrete aptitudes (e.g., analytic reasoning, vocabulary derivation skills, grammatical insight) so those aptitudes can be directly taught and tested.
